items.followUp: Describe the setup and three observations of the gold-foil experiment.

rubric.why: The experiment used a source of alpha particles.
rubric.description: Identifies the alpha-particle source.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a radioactive or alpha-particle source.

rubric.why: A thin metal foil was the target in the experiment.
rubric.description: Names the thin foil target.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the gold foil (or thin foil).

rubric.why: A screen was used to detect where the alpha particles went.
rubric.description: Identifies the detecting screen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the zinc sulphide or fluorescent screen.

rubric.why: Most particles passed through the foil without changing direction.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed straight through.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: A smaller number of particles changed direction, and a very few were reflected backwards.
rubric.description: States the deflection and backward-scattering observations.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that some were deflected and a very few bounced back.

modelAnswer: A narrow beam of alpha particles from a radioactive source was directed at a very thin gold foil.
A zinc sulphide fluorescent screen surrounding the foil was used to detect the alpha particles by flashes.
Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil without deflection.
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
A very small number were deflected backwards, nearly in the direction from which they had come.

items.followUp: Write four differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: A compound has a fixed composition, unlike a mixture.
rubric.description: Gives the difference in composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that compounds have a fixed ratio or composition while mixtures can have variable proportions.

rubric.why: The substances in a compound are chemically joined; those in a mixture are not.
rubric.description: Gives the difference in how the substances are combined.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting chemical combination in compounds with physical mixing in mixtures.

rubric.why: A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements, while mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.description: Gives the difference in properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this contrast.

rubric.why: The two types of material are separated by different methods.
rubric.description: Gives the difference in separation methods.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that compounds require chemical methods to separate their elements, whereas mixtures can be separated by physical methods.

modelAnswer: A compound has a fixed composition and its elements are present in a definite ratio; a mixture can have its components in any proportion.
The elements in a compound are chemically combined; the substances in a mixture are physically mixed and not chemically combined.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; the components of a mixture retain their individual properties.
The elements of a compound can be separated only by chemical methods; the components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.

items.followUp: Explain hydrogen bonding in water and show how it occurs between two water molecules.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding is an attractive force involving a hydrogen atom.
rubric.description: Defines hydrogen bonding as an attraction involving hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as an attractive force involving hydrogen.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding occurs when hydrogen is associated with a highly electronegative atom, commonly O, N or F.
rubric.description: Identifies the electronegative atom involved.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming an appropriate atom or stating that it is highly electronegative.

rubric.why: The attraction is between neighbouring molecules.
rubric.description: Identifies the between-molecule nature of the bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the attraction links different molecules.

rubric.why: Water is a standard example of hydrogen bonding.
rubric.description: Gives water as an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming water or H2O.

rubric.why: The example should show or state that the hydrogen of one water molecule is attracted to the oxygen of another.
rubric.description: Explains the water-molecule interaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the H···O attraction between neighbouring water molecules, preferably shown with a dotted line.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular force of attraction involving a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom.
It commonly occurs when hydrogen is bonded to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine and is attracted to an electronegative atom of a neighbouring molecule.
In water, the hydrogen atom of one molecule is attracted to the oxygen atom of another water molecule.
This attraction between neighbouring water molecules is called a hydrogen bond.
It can be represented as H—O—H···O—H, where the dotted line shows the hydrogen bond between molecules.

rubric.why: The definition refers to the average mass of atoms of the element.
rubric.description: Identifies the atomic mass being compared.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for referring to the average mass of an atom of the element.

rubric.why: Relative atomic mass uses one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom as its reference.
rubric.description: Gives the carbon-12 reference scale.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the comparison with 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom's mass.

modelAnswer: Relative atomic mass is the average mass of an atom of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
It has no unit because it is a relative value.

items.followUp: How many particles are present in 2 moles of a substance?

rubric.why: One mole contains Avogadro's number of particles.
rubric.description: States the number of particles in one mole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving approximately 6.02 × 10^23 particles.

rubric.why: A mole counts specified elementary entities of a substance.
rubric.description: Identifies what the mole counts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is an amount containing that number of particles or entities.

modelAnswer: A mole is the amount of a substance that contains 6.02 × 10^23 elementary particles, such as atoms, molecules or ions.
This number is called Avogadro's number.

items.followUp: Define electronegativity and use HCl to illustrate it.

rubric.why: Electronegativity describes an atom's attraction for electrons in a bond.
rubric.description: Defines the tendency to attract electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an atom attracts or pulls electrons.

rubric.why: The definition concerns the shared electrons of a chemical bond, and the example should illustrate this.
rubric.description: Specifies the shared bonding electrons and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying the shared pair in a bond and illustrating it with an appropriate example, such as chlorine attracting the shared pair more strongly than hydrogen in HCl.

modelAnswer: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself.
For example, in HCl the chlorine atom attracts the shared pair of electrons more strongly than the hydrogen atom.

items.followUp: Define a chemical property and give one example.

rubric.why: A physical property can be observed or measured without changing the substance's chemical composition.
rubric.description: Defines a physical property.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it can be observed or measured without a chemical change.

rubric.why: An example demonstrates a property that can be observed without making a new substance.
rubric.description: Gives an example of a physical property.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example, such as colour, density or melting point.

modelAnswer: A physical property is a characteristic that can be observed or measured without changing the chemical composition of a substance.
For example, the melting point of ice is a physical property.

items.followUp: Name the two kinds of particles found in the nucleus of an atom.

rubric.why: Protons are one kind of nucleon.
rubric.description: Names protons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying protons.

rubric.why: Neutrons are the other kind of nucleon; nucleons are located in the nucleus.
rubric.description: Names neutrons and identifies nucleons as nuclear particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying neutrons; accept the point when the answer identifies protons and neutrons as the particles in the nucleus.

modelAnswer: Nucleons are the particles present in the nucleus of an atom.
They are protons and neutrons.
